title: Customising and building — the code, then the result

slides.title: The edit, then the result
slides.lede: Every pair in this deck is one change and what it did. The left-hand slide is the actual edit — a bootstrap fragment, a manifest fragment, a TypeScript component. The right-hand slide is a real screenshot of the running application afterwards.

slides.title: Two tracks, both real

items.title: Track A — customise the shipped app
items.text: Change a configuration package's bootstrap or manifest fragment. **No rebuild, no fork.** The same bundle renders it on the next load.

items.title: Track B — build a UI from scratch
items.text: A separate application on the published package. Write a component, add a route, register a nav entry. **Their repo, their build.**

slides.footnote: Every screenshot was produced by `scripts/demo-deck/capture.mjs`, which asserts each image's own content before releasing it — so a slide captioned "the label changed" cannot carry a picture where it did not.

slides.title: Where we start
slides.lede: The product as shipped, against a real Nuxeo repository, with an **empty manifest**. Columns read `Title, Modified, Last Contributor`. Everything after this slide is a change to this app.
slides.footnote: The manifest response is reset to our defaults alone, with no customer fragment, for this capture on purpose. An earlier run had left column overrides applied, which would have made a customised screen look like the baseline.

slides.title: Make it their product, in a file
slides.lede: Branding is **Layer 0, a bootstrap fragment**, not part of the manifest — `runtime-manifest.ts` has no `branding` or `themes` key at all. Confusing the two stores is the most common way this goes wrong.

blocks.code: // agentic-ui-config/bootstrap.json in the customer's own package — // an upgrade of ours leaves it in force. { "branding": { "applicationTitle": "Acme Insurance", "documentTitle": "Acme Insurance" }, "defaultThemeId": "acme", "themes": [{ "id": "acme", "label": "Acme Brand", "base": "light", // CSS custom properties applied to <html> — no rebuild "tokens": { "--mat-sys-primary": "rgb(123, 47, 247)", "--agentic-pill-radius": "4px" } }] }

slides.footnote: Every key is optional; anything omitted falls back to the compiled-in value, so an untouched file behaves exactly like no file. `branding.logo` names an image the package ships as an asset and replaces the Satori marks; there is **no favicon key**. Say that plainly rather than being asked.

slides.title: Make it speak the customer's language
slides.lede: Not a settings heading — the words their users read all day. Every one of the **fourteen** nav ids the product renders by default is relabellable, reorderable and hideable by id, and the same mechanism renames list columns.

blocks.code: // the manifest fragment in the customer's configuration package "overrides": { // their words, on the surfaces users live in "app.navbar.browse": { "label": "Claim Files", "order": 10 }, "app.navbar.collections": { "label": "Policies", "order": 20 }, "app.navbar.tasks": { "label": "Underwriting Queue", "order": 30 }, "app.navbar.favorites": { "label": "Flagged Claims", "order": 40 }, "app.navbar.expiredQueue": { "label": "Lapsed Policies", "order": 50 }, "app.navbar.recentlyViewed": { "label": "Recent Activity", "order": 60 }, // irrelevant to this customer — gone, not greyed "app.navbar.knowledgeDiscovery": { "visible": false }, "app.navbar.assets": { "visible": false }, // the list speaks it too "app.documentList.lastContributor": { "label": "Adjuster", "order": 5 } }

slides.footnote: Two routes to navigation text, not one. `overrides.<id>.label` is one literal in every language; Layer 0 `labels["nav.item.<slug>"]` is per-locale, resolved through each descriptor's `labelKey`. Set both and the override wins, leaving the `labels` entry inert.

slides.title: The result: it reads like their product

items.label: After
items.alt: Insurance vocabulary throughout the navigation and columns

slides.footnote: Twelve nav entries renamed or removed and a column relabelled, from one manifest fragment. Same bundle, same deployment, no rebuild — and the nav rail is expanded here on purpose, because collapsed it hides every label behind an icon.

slides.title: Shape the column picker, not just the table
slides.lede: Two different controls, and the difference matters to an administrator. `disabled` **takes a column away from the user entirely**. `hiddenByDefault` **offers it, starting unchecked**.

blocks.code: "overrides": { // rename, and move it to the front "app.documentList.lastContributor": { "label": "Adjuster", "order": 5 } }, "slots": { "documentList": [ // gone from the picker — the user cannot turn it back on { "id": "app.documentList.state", "disabled": true }, // in the picker, but starts unchecked { "id": "app.documentList.version", "hiddenByDefault": true } ] }

slides.footnote: `hiddenByDefault` and `sortable` are honoured in `slots.documentList`, **not** in `overrides` — `overrides` reads only `order`, `label`, `rule` and `visible`, and silently drops the rest. The same descriptor ids drive the product's own list and upstream's `hxp-document-list`.

slides.title: The result: the picker, opened

blocks.alt: Column settings panel open, showing Version offered but unchecked and State absent

slides.footnote: Read the panel, not the table: **Adjuster** is the renamed column, **Version** is present but unchecked, and **State is absent altogether**. A screenshot of the resulting table shows the outcome but cannot show the control — which is why this slide opens it.

slides.title: Add whole pages, and route to them
slides.lede: A manifest is not limited to renaming what ships. It can contribute **routes** as well as entries, resolving a registered component by id — so a customer places their own pages wherever they want them, as many as they want.

blocks.code: // one-time, in code (Layer 2): make the page addressable by id components: { 'app.page.contracts': () => import('../features/contracts/contracts-page.component') .then((m) => m.ContractsPageComponent), } // from then on it is all manifest (Layer 1) — no rebuild "slots": { "routes": [ { "id": "app.page.contracts", "path": "contracts" } ], "navbar": [ { "label": "Contracts", "path": "/contracts", "icon": "gavel", "order": 15 }, { "label": "Renewals", "path": "/contracts", "icon": "autorenew", "order": 16 }, { "label": "Compliance", "path": "/contracts", "icon": "verified", "order": 17 } ] }

slides.footnote: Stated honestly: the **component** must be compiled in — that is the one-time Layer 2 step. Placing it, routing it, naming it and rule-gating it are Layer 1 and need no build. The `routes` slot went live on 2026-08-31; `app.page.contracts` was registered because until then the product shipped **no** component a manifest route could resolve, so the slot was live and unusable here.

slides.eyebrow: Track A · 5 of 5 — actions and rules
slides.title: Add actions, and gate them declaratively
slides.lede: Two different gates, and the difference is the point. `rule` **removes** the action when it does not hold. `enabledRule` **keeps it and greys it out**. Same declarative mechanism, two user experiences, no code.

blocks.code: "bulk-actions": [ { "id": "acme.bulkActions.archive", "label": "Archive", "icon": "inventory_2", "order": 15 }, { "id": "acme.bulkActions.merge", "label": "Merge selected", "icon": "merge", "order": 25, "rule": "app.rules.hasMultipleSelection" }, // removes { "id": "acme.bulkActions.review", "label": "Send for review", "icon": "rate_review", "order": 26, "enabledRule": "app.rules.hasMultipleSelection" } // disables ]

slides.footnote: `app.bulkActions.publish` is hidden by an override in the same edit. Adding a seventh bulk action used to be a button, an `@Output()` and a shell handler across three files in two projects; it is now two registrations.

slides.eyebrow: Track B · 1 of 5 — wiring a page
slides.title: A page is three edits, and the platform does the rest
slides.lede: This is the whole mechanism for adding a surface to an app built on the published package. Nothing here is scaffolding you have to understand — a component, a lazy route, a nav descriptor.

blocks.code: // 1 — the component. pages/case-file/case-file.ts // Only published entry points, and that is the whole contract. import { DocumentDetailService, SearchService } from '@nuxeo-satori/platform/nuxeo-client'; import { DocumentViewerComponent, ShareDialogComponent } from '@nuxeo-satori/platform/ui'; @Component({ selector: 'app-case-file', standalone: true, /* … */ }) export class CaseFileComponent { /* … */ } // 2 — the route. app.routes.ts — lazy, so its chunk is only // fetched when someone actually navigates here. { path: 'case-file', loadComponent: () => import('./pages/case-file/case-file').then((m) => m.CaseFileComponent) } // 3 — the nav entry. extensions/template-extensions.ts { id: 'template.navbar.caseFile', label: 'Case File', path: '/case-file', icon: 'folder_special', order: 15, // rule-gated: with no credential every request 401s, and a link // that can only fail is worse than no link rule: 'template.rules.isSignedIn' }

slides.footnote: `order: 15` places it between two existing entries without restating the list — the same ten-spacing convention the product uses. The rule is registered in the same file and declared **fail-closed**, so an unregistered build hides the entry rather than offering it.

slides.eyebrow: Track B · 2 of 5 — an ECM surface
slides.title: Search, metadata, preview and actions
slides.lede: What a content application actually needs, and where each part comes from. The **two-step** is the bit worth noticing: a search row is not a document.

blocks.code: // FIND — search() answers SearchResultItem: flat, list-shaped. // It carries no properties bag and no blob, so it cannot feed // a metadata panel or a preview. this.search.search({ pageSize: 40 }) // METADATA — selecting a row fetches the FULL document. this.documents.getFullDocument(item.id) // PREVIEW — fetch the blob through the service, wrap it in an // object URL, and revoke it. Never bind a Nuxeo URL to [src]: // that request leaves the auth interceptor behind and 401s. this.documents.fetchBlob(doc.uid).subscribe((data) => { this.rawObjectUrl = URL.createObjectURL(data); this.blobUrl.set(sanitizer.bypassSecurityTrustResourceUrl(this.rawObjectUrl)); }); destroyRef.onDestroy(() => URL.revokeObjectURL(this.rawObjectUrl)); // ACTIONS — the platform's dialogs; the host supplies how bytes // are fetched, because the platform never builds an auth header. this.dialog.open(ShareDialogComponent, { data: { title, url } }); this.dialog.open(ExportDialogComponent, { data: { exportFn } });

slides.footnote: The revoke is the half that gets forgotten, and it has to happen **on replacement as well as on destroy** — otherwise every document a user clicks leaks a blob for the life of the page.

slides.eyebrow: Track B · 4 of 5 — what comes for free
slides.title: The components, and a screen that explains itself

items.label: Diagnostics
items.alt: Diagnostics page listing configuration sources and every registered extension id

slides.footnote: Diagnostics is the screen to open when a customisation does not appear: it distinguishes "the manifest did not load" from "the id is not registered" from "a rule denied it" — three failures that look identical in the UI. Four Nx generators scaffold the rest; the three contribution generators write registrations but **no specs**.

slides.title: Four commands that write the boilerplate
slides.lede: A customer does not start from a blank file. One command scaffolds a whole extension library; three more add a rule, an action or a component to an existing one.

blocks.code: // 1 — a whole extension library, owner-prefixed npx nx g extension-library contoso-extensions --owner=contoso // 2 — a rule: visibility logic the manifest can reference by id npx nx g extension-rule is-underwriter --library=contoso-extensions // 3 — an action: a handler a manifest can place in any slot npx nx g extension-action export-policy --library=contoso-extensions // 4 — a component: a lazily-loaded panel or page, addressable by id npx nx g extension-component claim-summary --library=contoso-extensions

slides.footnote: The generators ship **inside** the published package, so a customer runs them against their own repo rather than ours. All four commands above were run with `--dry-run` to produce the next slide, and the working tree was verified unchanged afterwards.

slides.title: What the commands actually produce
slides.lede: Real output, captured from the four runs — not a description of them.

blocks.code: $ nx g extension-library contoso-extensions --owner=contoso CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/project.json CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/README.md CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/src/index.ts CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/src/lib/extensions.ts CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/src/lib/extensions.spec.ts CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/src/lib/panel/contoso-panel.ts CREATE libs/extensions/contoso-extensions/src/lib/rules.service.ts … 14 files in total, plus UPDATE tsconfig.base.json $ nx g extension-rule is-underwriter --library=… UPDATE .../src/lib/extensions.ts // registers the id UPDATE .../src/lib/rules.service.ts // where the logic goes $ nx g extension-component claim-summary --library=… CREATE .../src/lib/claim-summary/claim-summary.ts CREATE .../src/lib/claim-summary/claim-summary.html CREATE .../src/lib/claim-summary/claim-summary.scss UPDATE .../src/lib/extensions.ts // registers + lazy-loads it

slides.footnote: **Be honest if asked:** the library generator writes a spec; the three contribution generators write registrations but **no specs**. They also shipped broken once — every insertion landed inside the marker comment, and lint, typecheck and six specs all passed. `insertAboveMarker` now asserts, after writing, that the inserted line exists as a line of its own.

slides.title: The customer points an AI agent at it
slides.lede: Layer 3 makes Layer 2 cheap, and it **ships inside the package** — a customer's agent reads it in their own checkout, with no access to our source.

items.title: `AGENTS.md` — written **to** the agent
items.text: The layer cost table, the four traps, and rules aimed at agents: never edit the platform; prefer a generator; an ID is a public contract.

items.title: `extension-reference.md` — every addressable ID
items.text: With each slot's **real state**. An agent that guesses an id gets a silent no-op; this is how it stops guessing.

items.title: Four generators — conforming code by default
items.text: Registration, marker comments and a spec, so the first attempt already follows the conventions.

items.title: A runnable guardrail — the agent's own check
items.text: Not a review checklist. An exit code, in the customer's CI.

slides.footnote: The rule the layer exists to enforce, quoted from the file: **"Never fork to change something a layer already addresses."** With the corollary that keeps us honest — a gap at every layer is **a gap worth raising, not a reason to fork**.

slides.title: Why an agent can be trusted here: it gets told off
slides.lede: An agent that only compiles its work will ship something that registers nothing. So the harness closes the loop with a check the agent runs itself — and the failure names the file, the bad import, and the five entry points it should have used.

blocks.code: $ npm run beta:customer-guardrails # the agent's own work, clean check-extension-library: pass — libs/extensions/acme-extensions (owner `acme`), 6 source file(s), 2 spec file(s). $ # …and the same check on a library that reached into internals check-extension-library: FAIL - src/lib/rules.service.ts imports `@nuxeo-satori/platform/extensions/internal/rule-registry`, which is not a published entry point. Published: @nuxeo-satori/platform, /extensions, /app-config, /nuxeo-client, /ui A deep path into internals will break without that being a breaking change.

slides.footnote: **eslint cannot enforce this**, and says so in its own config comment: a path alias makes a supported import and a raw internal one the same edge in the dependency graph. This script is what actually holds the support boundary — which is why it ships to the customer instead of living in our CI.
